title: How Can We Improve Our Judgment
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece breaks down good judgment into three learnable steps: maintaining objectivity by holding personal bias in check, gathering the widest possible range of information and viewpoints before narrowing them, and finally weighing that information for plausibility and feasibility. The author argues judgment is under-taught relative to its importance to leadership success, and frames the three-step approach less as a formula for a single decision than as a practice routine that improves judgment over time, especially for people prone to premature conviction.
points: Good judgment is described as central to leadership success yet rarely taught explicitly.
The first step is holding personal bias and self-interest in check before evaluating information.
The second step is deliberately widening the range of information and viewpoints before narrowing them.
The third step weighs the gathered information for plausibility and practical feasibility.
quotes: Good judgment comes from experience and experience comes from bad judgment, or so goes the well-known quote.
Technically speaking, judgment is the ability to weigh complex information and competing ideas and reach a reasonable conclusion.
This is why people with strong convictions, committed ideologies, and deep-seated assumptions often make poor judgments.
People with poor judgment often limit the possibilities too quickly or land on a viewpoint before considering the options.
Our judgment evolves as we open the mind before narrowing it.
